title: Club sandwich
subtitle: Three-tier toasted sandwich with chicken, bacon, and tomato
excerpt: A club sandwich is three slices of toasted white bread layered with sliced chicken, crisp bacon, lettuce, tomato, and mayonnaise, held together with cocktail sticks and cut into quarters. It is a hotel and diner classic that requires no cooking beyond the bacon if you have leftover chicken.
sourceNotes: American diner and club tradition. The club sandwich appeared in American cookery from the late nineteenth century and became a hotel and club dining staple. Documented as a club-house specialty in Fannie Farmer, The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book (1896), Project Gutenberg.

content.text: A club sandwich uses three slices of toasted bread and two layers of filling. The lower layer is chicken and the middle bread; the upper layer is bacon, tomato, and lettuce. Mayonnaise goes on every slice. Held together with cocktail sticks and cut diagonally into four triangles, it is as much an architectural exercise as a sandwich.

items.prepNote: cooked and sliced, or leftover roast chicken

content.text: Cook the {{streaky-bacon}} of bacon until crisp. If using raw chicken breasts, season and pan-fry or poach. Slice once cooled.

Spread {{mayonnaise}} of mayonnaise on one side of all 6 toasted slices. On the first slice, lay sliced chicken. Cover with the second (middle) slice, mayonnaise-side down. Spread more mayonnaise on the top side of the middle slice, then lay on the bacon, sliced tomato (seasoned with salt), and lettuce leaves.
Press the third slice on top, mayonnaise-side down. Push a cocktail stick through each quarter before cutting diagonally. Serve with crisps.

items.cause: Cocktail sticks not in place before cutting.
items.fix: Insert 4 cocktail sticks in a square pattern before cutting diagonally through all layers.

content.text: Turkey in place of chicken is the American deli version. Avocado adds creaminess to the bacon layer. A thin spread of Dijon on the middle slice instead of extra mayonnaise adds sharpness.

The club sandwich was a fixture of American hotel dining rooms and gentleman's clubs from the late nineteenth century. The three-slice format made it a status sandwich: more generous than a standard two-slice construction. It remains one of the most widely ordered sandwiches in American hotel restaurants.
